extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newspaper editors, journalism students, and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and explanatory criteria for how newspapers select, gather, and present news—covering newsworthiness, sources, audience targeting, institutional routines, and economic pressures on daily journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of metropolitan dailies as key news sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The key metropolitan dailies (about 175 in cities over 100,000) constitute the press for 'general news' and act as local reporters for newspapers of other cities via press associations and special services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These papers gather and distribute news that other papers (rural or special press) take; international and national coverage often depends on a few metropolitan dailies and wire services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic audience determines support for general news
rubrics_metrics.description: Roughly speaking, the economic support for general news gathering is in the price paid for advertised goods by the fairly prosperous sections of cities—the buying publics among whom it pays best to advertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers orient content to the interests of advertisers' customer base; understanding the advertiser-supported clientele explains editorial choices and what will sustain news operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty as source of editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper that can really depend upon the loyalty of its readers is as independent as a newspaper can be, given the economics of modern journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More readers dilute individual advertisers' influence; cultivating a devoted band of constant readers increases independence from advertisers. Betraying readers for advertisers risks loss of that power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers judge newspapers by treatment of news within their experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of us tends to judge a newspaper by its treatment of that part of the news in which we feel ourselves involved; if the newspaper gives a satisfactory account of that which we think we know, we trust it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To win and retain readers, prioritize accuracy and sympathetic handling of matters that intersect with readers' business, church, party, and local life.

rubrics_metrics.name: No legal standing of general readers to correct news; limited external check
rubrics_metrics.description: The general reader has no standing in law if he thinks he is being misled; only the aggrieved party can sue for slander or libel and must prove material injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because disinterested readers lack legal remedy, mechanisms beyond litigation (e.g., non-official competent tribunals) would be useful for sifting charges of untruthfulness and unfairness in general news.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires an overt act or definable manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a series of events become news they usually have to make themselves noticeable in some more or less overt act; there must be a manifestation with unmistakable form (bankruptcy filing, arrest, bill introduction, speech, vote, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events often must be 'objectified'—fixed, measured, named—before they can be reported as news; reporters look for such points of fixation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of record-keeping machinery increases news certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a very direct relation between the certainty of news and the system of record: where machinery of record exists (stock exchange tickers, election returns, births/deaths registries), news can be reported with dependable accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on official records and established reporting machinery where available; topics lacking such systems are intrinsically less certain and more debatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics lacking objective records are debatable and prone to opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects involving states of mind, personality, motives, public opinion, policies, internal trade and many social conditions lack consistent, objective records; therefore news on these subjects is bound to be debatable or reported as conventional opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reporting on unscored subjects cautiously, avoid definitive assertions, and make clear the limits of evidence; investigative work or official signals are often needed to make such topics newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter routines and beats concentrate coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers have watchers stationed at certain places (Police Headquarters, Coroner's Office, County Clerk, City Hall, White House, etc.) and work by a standardized routine rather than attempting to witness all happenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize coverage around beats and predictable sources to capture public acts and records; cultivate relationships at these institutions to uncover news efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the ability to see news (news sense) before overt events
rubrics_metrics.description: A good journalist will find news oftener than a hack; he can recognize news before it culminates in a fully overt act (e.g., noticing a dangerous lean in a building before it falls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop judgment and familiarity with patterns so reporters can anticipate and frame emerging events rather than only record completed acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents filter and shape news for employers' interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity men present reporters a clear picture of a situation shaped to make the public see what the employer wishes; they act as censor and propagandist, responsible to employers rather than to the whole truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of accepting press-agent material uncritically; verify claims and understand the employer's interest shaping the narrative. Recognize that many direct channels to news are now filtered through publicity agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactured 'stunts' as a route to free publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The publicity man knows virtues are not news unless they 'jut right out of the routine'; to get free publicity he arranges stunts or creates situations that entangle clients with events that are already news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should detect staged actions intended to create news and distinguish them from spontaneously occurring news; editors should assess whether the stunt legitimately conveys public-interest information.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-depth investigative reporting is resource-intensive and rare for dailies
rubrics_metrics.description: To make plausible a report that complex conditions are bad (e.g., industrial conditions), one needs a staff of investigators, time, and space; such work is beyond the resources of a normal daily press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of daily newspapers for producing extended investigations; when such reporting is required, allocate special resources or rely on organizations able to fund deeper inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value increases with disruption to readers' lives or public order
rubrics_metrics.description: If a stoppage involves a service on which readers depend, or if a breach of order occurs, the news value increases; events that interfere with readers' routines are more likely to be prominent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsworthiness partly by potential direct impact on the readership and by whether an event threatens public order or essential services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters tend to report overt phases and stereotyped bulletins in complex disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: In strikes and similar disputes, reporters often report the overt act (walkout, arrest) and rely on stereotyped bulletins; the deeper issues and causes may be barely mentioned or absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of this routine tendency and make effort to investigate underlying causes and context rather than allowing stories to be reduced to abstract catchwords and stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: News is selective representation, not a mirror of social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first instance, the news is not a mirror of social conditions, but the report of an aspect that has obtruded itself; it tells when some sprout breaks the surface, not how the seed germinates underground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and reporters should expect and compensate for the selectivity of news; reporters should attempt to provide context where possible to indicate what lies beneath the overt event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational economics and career incentives shape reporting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting is often the most poorly paid and least regarded branch of newspaper work; able men move on to specialty work, signed correspondence, or executive positions, limiting the development of corporate traditions in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To raise standards, news organizations should recognize and reward reporting careers, cultivate professional traditions, and provide structures that retain and develop talented reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use institutional or official interventions as triggers for reporting complex issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad conditions often do not become news until an official body (Board of Health) reports or the workers organize and make demands; such institutional signals make the issue reportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor official reports, institutional data, and organized public actions as legitimate triggers for in-depth stories on complex social problems; seek corroboration rather than relying only on stereotypes.
